title: Nvidia's big bet on physical AI aims for safer robotaxis, humanoid robots
content:
Investors bullish on AI data centers may be fueling Nvidia’s multitrillion-dollar market capitalization, but the AI chipmaker has also bet billions of dollars on physical AI technologies such as robotics and self-driving cars. Part of that gambit has involved developing a full-stack safety system that companies can build upon to reduce the risk of their machines harming nearby people.
Nvidia’s Halos system launched in 2025 with hardware and software tools to help developers implement guardrails in self-driving cars and other autonomous vehicles. Then the company expanded its safety architecture to more physical AI technologies by announcing Nvidia Halos for Robotics in June 2026—with the goal of enabling safe deployments of autonomous mobile robots in warehouses, humanoid robots walking around inside a factory, or even surgical robots.
“Now the AI models are getting capable, the robot hardware is getting capable, and a thing we thought is going to be the next bottleneck is safety,” Amit Goel, head of robotics ecosystem and edge computing at Nvidia, told Ars. “So that’s why we launched our Halos for Robotics to unlock the capability of these systems.”
The expanded safety offering for robotics comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the physical AI business as already driving nearly $10 billion in annual revenue for the company during an appearance on the All-In Podcast in March 2026. Huang began highlighting physical AI as Nvidia’s second-most important growth category in 2025.
The tech giant has also invested directly in multiple robotics companies, including the humanoid robotics startups Agility Robotics and Figure AI, along with companies developing robotics foundation models. Nvidia has even partnered with the Chinese humanoid robotics company Unitree to provide an “open humanoid robot reference design” for researchers.
Expanding safety from AVs to robots
So what does Nvidia’s full-stack safety system for robotics involve? It starts with hardware, such as the Nvidia IGX Thor computing module for robotics and industrial applications that has an independent processor dedicated to safety-related workloads. “In the context of physical AI, you need to have your functional system and your safety system all running on the same silicon,” Goel said.

report.summary: Nvidia is extending its Halos full-stack safety architecture from self-driving cars to robots, betting safety tooling will unlock commercial deployment of humanoid robots and robotaxis.
report.background: Nvidia's valuation is dominated by AI data-center demand, but the company has spent years and billions positioning 'physical AI' — robotics and autonomous vehicles — as its next major growth engine. CEO Jensen Huang began calling physical AI Nvidia's second-most important growth category in 2025, and by March 2026 said it already generated nearly $10 billion in annual revenue. The obstacle is no longer raw capability: perception models, robot foundation models, and hardware have improved rapidly, but regulators, insurers, and customers still demand proof that machines will not injure people nearby. Nvidia's answer is a layered safety stack — hardware, software, and certification tooling — that manufacturers can build on rather than reinventing. It mirrors how the auto industry converged on shared safety standards (ISO 26262, SOTIF) and how Nvidia's CUDA became a default platform: whoever supplies the safety layer also supplies the silicon underneath it.
key_points: Nvidia launched Halos in 2025 as a hardware-plus-software safety stack for autonomous vehicles, adding guardrails such as redundant sensing, fail-safe compute, and safety monitors. In June 2026 it announced Halos for Robotics, extending the same architecture to warehouse robots, humanoid workers, and even surgical robots.

Nvidia's Amit Goel frames safety as the emerging constraint: models and robot hardware are now capable enough, but without certified safety layers, deployments stall. Halos is positioned as the unlock rather than a feature add-on.

Physical AI is already material business. Jensen Huang said in March 2026 that robotics and autonomous vehicle work drives nearly $10 billion in annual revenue, making it Nvidia's second-most important growth category after data centers.

Nvidia is investing across the ecosystem rather than going alone — backing humanoid startups Agility Robotics and Figure AI, funding robotics foundation model companies, and partnering with China's Unitree on an open humanoid robot reference design for researchers.

The hardware foundation is the IGX Thor computing module for robotics and industrial use, which pairs application compute with an independent processor dedicated to safety workloads — letting functional and safety systems run on the same silicon, which Goel calls essential for physical AI.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Nvidia is repeating its CUDA playbook: if Halos becomes the reference safety layer, robot makers standardize on Nvidia silicon by default, deepening the moat beyond data centers. For developers, a full-stack safety offering lowers the cost of building compliant autonomous systems — but also nudges them into Nvidia's software ecosystem, trading flexibility for certification shortcuts. For regular users, the practical effect is timing: certified safety layers are what let a warehouse robot or robotaxi move from pilot to public streets and factory floors, and what insurers and regulators will point to when granting approvals. The risk is concentration — a single vendor's safety assumptions becoming the industry's default, and a slow certification path for anyone who deviates.
report.tools: To follow along, look at Nvidia Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab for robot simulation and training, Isaac ROS for GPU-accelerated robotics middleware, and Omniverse for digital-twin testing. On hardware, watch the IGX Thor module and Jetson line. Open-source options worth trying include ROS 2, MuJoCo and LeRobot for learning-based manipulation, and Unitree's open humanoid reference design for research platforms.
